Good evening. Since Class 1 you have carried a list of nine warning signs about Kalmia: the roaster computer on Windows 10 with a vendor's remote access, the flat network of the roastery, the file server whose backup disk never leaves it, the cameras that still have their factory passwords, and five more. On Thursday you turned threats into the first rows of a threat catalogue. Tonight we look at the other side of every risk: the weaknesses that a threat would use.

Topic 4 is the evidence step of the risk analysis. A warning sign is something somebody said in an interview. A vulnerability is a weakness that we can show: a line in a scan, a setting on a screen, a date on a vendor's page. Before a weakness enters the risk register of Lab 3, it must be written with its evidence. That is what you will practise in the three lessons of this hour.

Lesson 1 looks at the network itself: how it is divided, what it exposes, who can reach it from outside and what the Wi-Fi reaches. Lesson 2 looks at the software that runs on it: programs whose vendor has stopped publishing fixes, fixes that were published but never installed, and products still running with the settings they had in the box. Lesson 3 teaches you to read the document that brings most of this evidence together: the vulnerability scan report. Quiz 2 follows the lecture.

▣ Slide 2 — The one fact to rememberThe one fact to remember

A vulnerability is a property of a system; a risk factor is that vulnerability in its context. The same weakness is a small problem on an isolated device and a serious one on a flat network, on the Internet or on the roaster computer. Every weakness you record tonight needs three things: the evidence that proves it, the path that makes it reachable, and the asset that would suffer.

Lesson 1 — Threats and vulnerabilities related to network architecture

Segmentation, exposed services, remote access and wireless — and how each weakness is proved with evidence
0:04 – 0:24
▣ Slide 7 — Threats and vulnerabilities related to network architecture

Read-aloud script — 13 minutes

▣ Slide 8 — From warning signs to vulnerabilities

From warning signs to vulnerabilities

Let us start with three words that you will use until the end of the course. A vulnerability is a weakness in an information system, in a security procedure, in an internal control or in the way something was implemented, which a threat source could exploit or trigger. That definition comes from NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1, the guide for conducting risk assessments that we met in Class 1. Notice the word could: a vulnerability is a possibility, not an incident.

The same guide calls a risk factor any characteristic that is used as an input to determine the level of risk: the threat, the vulnerability, the impact, the likelihood, and a fifth one that matters a great deal tonight, the predisposing condition. A predisposing condition is a property of the organization or of its architecture that makes it more likely — or less likely — that a threat, once started, produces harm. A flat network is the typical example. It is not a flaw in any single product; it is a design choice that makes every flaw on every device more dangerous.

The competency of this course, EZ02, asks for two things in this part of Topic 4: an accurate identification of threats and vulnerabilities related to network architecture (criterion 3.1) and an exhaustive identification of vulnerable or obsolete applications and services (criterion 3.2). Lesson 1 covers the first, Lesson 2 the second, and Lesson 3 shows you the document that supplies most of the evidence for both.

▣ Slide 9 — Network architecture: four questions

Network architecture: four questions

Network architecture is the arrangement of the devices, links, address ranges and zones of a network, together with the rules that decide which traffic may pass between them. An analyst does not need to configure a firewall to assess an architecture. You need to answer four questions, each with evidence: Who can talk to whom inside the network? What is listening, and to whom? Who can come in from outside, and how? What does the radio reach? Those four questions are the four families of this lesson: segmentation, exposed services, remote access and wireless.

▣ Slide 10 — Segmentation — the vocabulary

1 — Segmentation

Network segmentation is the division of a network into separate segments — usually separate IP (Internet Protocol) subnets carried on separate VLANs (virtual local area networks) — with a firewall or router between them that applies an access control list. A zone is a group of devices that share the same level of trust and the same protection needs. Traffic that stays inside the building is called east-west traffic; traffic that enters or leaves the organization is north-south traffic. A perimeter firewall controls north-south traffic. Only segmentation controls east-west traffic.

A flat network is a network with a single zone and no internal filtering: every device can reach every port of every other device. The consequence has a name in the MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) framework that you used on Thursday: lateral movement, the tactic by which an attacker who controls one device moves to the next. On a flat network, lateral movement needs no special technique, because nothing stands between the first device and the most valuable one.

▣ Slide 11 — Zones and deny by default (ITSG-38)

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security publishes a zoning model in ITSG-38. It separates the Public Zone, which is the Internet, from a Public Access Zone where Internet-facing services are placed — comparable to what many vendors call a DMZ (demilitarized zone) — from an Operations Zone for ordinary workstations and servers, and from Restricted Zones for the systems whose failure would stop the business. The principle between zones is deny by default: nothing passes unless a documented business need allows it, as NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-41 Rev. 1 explains for firewall policies.

▣ Slide 12 — Kalmia evidence — HQ-LAN is one flat zone

Now Kalmia. Lab 1 recorded one subnet for the whole head office, 192.168.10.0/24, with the note “internal filtering: none”. In that single network live the file server NAS-01, the administration workstation PC-IT-01, the roaster computer ROAST-PC, four cameras — two of them on factory passwords — the thermostat with a personal cloud account, the printers, the employees' phones, a data logger that nobody registered and a Wi-Fi extender that an employee plugged into a wall socket. Any one of those devices, once controlled by an attacker, can reach the file-sharing ports of NAS-01 and the remote desktop of PC-IT-01. That is warning sign W-02, now written as evidence: the zone table, the scan, and the list of devices that can reach each critical asset.

Two details deserve attention. First, ROAST-PC is operational technology (OT [operational technology]): a computer that controls a physical process, here the roaster. OT is kept apart from office IT (information technology) because its failure stops production and because it is often impossible to patch. Second, the cafés show the opposite case: the guest Wi-Fi Kalmia-Invite was tested on October 22 and its clients are isolated from each other and from the staff network. A control that works is recorded too — Lab 3 needs the existing controls to rate the likelihood.

▣ Slide 13 — Exposed services — three kinds

2 — Exposed services

A service is a program that waits for connections on a network port, a number from 0 to 65535 that identifies it on a host for TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) or UDP (User Datagram Protocol). A port is open when a service answers on it. A service is exposed when it can be reached from a network where it is not needed — the extreme case being the Internet, where automated scanners test every public address many times a day.

Three kinds of exposed services produce most architecture findings. The first is clear-text administration: Telnet on port 23, HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) on port 80, or an appliance's administration page on another HTTP port. Everything typed, including the password, crosses the network unencrypted. The second is remote administration reachable from everywhere: RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) on port 3389 or SSH (Secure Shell) on port 22 offered to every device instead of only to an administration host. The third is a management interface on the Internet: the login page of a firewall, a router or a storage appliance published to the whole world. The U.S. CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) Binding Operational Directive 23-02 requires federal agencies to remove such interfaces from the Internet or to protect them, because attackers search for them first.

▣ Slide 14 — Kalmia evidence — what the scan shows

The Kalmia scan of Lab 1 shows all three. Telnet answers on the switch SW-HQ and on the cameras CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4; HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) administration pages answer on the switch, the cameras, the printers, the extender and NAS-01 on port 5000; RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) and SMB (Server Message Block) answer on PC-IT-01, and SMB on the finance workstation PC-FIN-01. From the outside, the public address of FW-HQ shows the firewall's administration portal on port 443, and the web shop server accepts SSH (Secure Shell) on port 22 from any address. InfoNord says that only its office can log in to the portal. That may be true, but a statement is not evidence: until the firewall rule export shows the source restriction, the finding stays open.

▣ Slide 15 — Remote access — methods and four questions

3 — Remote access

Remote access is any means of using or controlling a system from outside its local network. The usual methods are a VPN (virtual private network), an encrypted tunnel that places a remote computer inside the network; RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) or SSH (Secure Shell) published directly; and remote-support tools — the agents used by managed service providers and vendors, which keep an outgoing connection to a relay server and let a technician take control from anywhere. When such a tool allows unattended access, nobody at the keyboard approves the session.

Remote access is evaluated with four questions: who connects, from where, with what authentication, and until when. The safeguards to look for are MFA (multi-factor authentication), a time limit or an end date, a record of every session, and a path that reaches only the system that needs support. Remember one point that surprises beginners: a remote-support agent does not need any open inbound port. The connection starts from the inside, so a port scan of the firewall shows nothing — the evidence comes from the contract, the installed software list and the firewall's outgoing traffic.

▣ Slide 16 — Kalmia's three remote paths

Kalmia has three remote paths. InfoNord administers FW-HQ through its portal with MFA (multi-factor authentication), a contract end date in June 2027 and logged sessions: the safeguards exist, and only the exposure of the portal remains to be verified. RoastTech Services controls ROAST-PC through the RoastLink agent, unattended, with no end date, and nobody at Kalmia knows whether MFA or a session log exists: that is warning sign W-01, confirmed and made precise. And the data logger LOG-ROAST-01 sends telemetry to a vendor cloud that was never declared — a channel that nobody approved, which could also carry commands back in. Inside the network, PC-IT-01 administers every device over HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), SSH (Secure Shell) and RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) without MFA, which makes Lucas Martin's workstation the most valuable target of the head office.

▣ Slide 17 — Wireless — modes and weaknesses

4 — Wireless

A WLAN (wireless local area network) is a wireless local area network; its name, broadcast by every access point, is the SSID (service set identifier). Small organizations usually protect it with WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) in personal mode, with a PSK (pre-shared key): a single password shared by everyone. That design has two weaknesses. A device that captures the connection exchange of one legitimate user can test passwords offline, without being noticed, so a short or common password falls quickly. And a shared password remains valid for every person who ever knew it, including employees who left. WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) replaces the exchange with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline guessing; enterprise mode, also called 802.1X (IEEE port-based network access control standard), gives each person an individual account checked by a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) server, so that a departure removes one account instead of forcing a password change for everyone.

Two more wireless weaknesses appear in small companies. A rogue access point is any radio connected to the network without authorization — often a consumer extender bought to improve coverage. An evil twin is an attacker's access point that broadcasts the same SSID (service set identifier) as the real one, to attract devices. And WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup), a push-button or PIN (personal identification number) method for joining a network, is still enabled by default on many ISP (Internet service provider) routers although its PIN mode has known weaknesses. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-153 covers the secure configuration and the monitoring of WLANs.

▣ Slide 18 — Kalmia's Wi-Fi evidence

At Kalmia, the Wi-Fi survey of Lab 1 found the staff network Kalmia-HQ bridged into the flat head-office network, protected by a WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) password that has not changed since March 15, 2022 — more than four years and many departures, with no offboarding checklist (W-06). It found the extender EXT-WH-01, absent from the inventory, repeating Kalmia-HQ into the warehouse with WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) on. And it found WPS enabled on the ISP (Internet service provider) router of the Plateau café. The guest network Kalmia-Invite, again, is a strength: isolated, and its password changed on October 1.

▣ Slide 19 — Writing a network-architecture risk factor

Writing a network-architecture risk factor

Each weakness becomes one row with six parts: an identifier (NA-01, NA-02 …), the family (segmentation, exposed service, remote access, wireless), the asset with its Lab 1 identifier, the weakness in one sentence, the evidence — the scan line, the zone table, the flow number, the survey date — and a provisional level. The level is provisional because Lab 3 will rate likelihood and impact properly. Tonight, Code example 1 does this automatically from the lab files and produces 24 rows, 8 of them rated HIGH. Your job, in Hours 2 and 3, is to check every one of them against its evidence.

Key terms to learn

vulnerability
a weakness in a system, a security procedure, an internal control or an implementation that a threat source could exploit or trigger (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-30 Rev. 1)
risk factor
a characteristic used as an input to determine the level of risk: threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood, predisposing condition
predisposing condition
a property of the organization or its architecture that increases or decreases the likelihood that a threat event causes harm (for example, a flat network)
network architecture
the arrangement of devices, links, address ranges and zones, with the rules that control traffic between them
network segmentation
the division of a network into separate segments (subnets, VLANs [virtual local area networks]) with filtering between them
zone
a group of devices sharing the same trust level and protection needs
flat network
a network with one zone and no internal filtering, where every device reaches every other device
east-west / north-south traffic
traffic inside the organization / traffic entering or leaving it
lateral movement
the attacker's progression from one compromised device to others (MITRE ATT&CK [Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge] tactic)
deny by default
the rule that blocks all traffic between zones unless a documented need allows it
service / port / exposed service
a program answering on a numbered port; exposed when reachable from a network where it is not needed
clear-text administration
administration over a protocol without encryption (Telnet, HTTP [Hypertext Transfer Protocol]), so passwords can be captured
management interface
the page or protocol used to administer a device; it must never be published on the Internet
remote access / unattended access
using or controlling a system from outside its network / a remote session that nobody on site approves
rogue access point / evil twin
an unauthorized radio connected to the network / an attacker's radio imitating a legitimate network name
operational technology (OT [operational technology])
computers and devices that control a physical process, such as the roaster

Micro-activity — Who can reach NAS-01? (3 min)

Look at Schematic 1 (left panel). In pairs, list every Kalmia device that can open a connection to NAS-01's file-sharing port (445/tcp) today. Then mark, for each one, the reason it should not be able to: it belongs to a family to separate (camera, IoT [Internet of Things], OT [operational technology], personal), or it is not in the inventory.

▣ Slide 21 — Real-life example — Kalmia's network-architecture risk factors

Real-life example — Kalmia's network-architecture risk factors — from the Lab 1 files to 24 evidence-based rows

Task

Using four lab files — the scan of the Kalmia lab replica (hosts, zones, open ports), the zone table, the declared remote-access flows and the Wi-Fi survey — identify Kalmia's network-architecture vulnerabilities in the four families of Lesson 1 and write each one as a risk factor with its evidence and a provisional level.

How it relates to this lecture

This is Lesson 1 applied to the case: segmentation (who can reach the critical assets), exposed services (clear-text and Internet-facing administration), remote access (safeguards of each outside path) and wireless (rogue radio, stale shared key, WPS [Wi-Fi Protected Setup]). It turns warning signs W-01, W-02, W-06 and W-07 into evidence.

Where it goes next (future labs)

Class 9 workshop (list of risk factors for the case organization — the 24 NA- rows are the 'network' starting list); Lab 3 — Risk register and prioritization (each NA- row receives a likelihood and an impact; starts November 14); Lab 4 — Risk treatment and prevention plan (segmentation, removal of exposed administration and control of vendor access are proposed there).

Lucas Martin sends you the four files collected for Lab 1 and one question from Nadia Roy: “If one device in the roastery is taken over, how far can the attacker go, and what else is open?” You answer with a table, not an opinion.

Read the result the way Nadia Roy will: one network decision — the absence of internal filtering — multiplies the effect of every other weakness. A camera with a factory password is a small problem on an isolated camera network; on HQ-LAN it is a path to the file server and to the administration workstation. That is why the first row of the list is a predisposing condition and not a product flaw.

▣ Slide 22 — Code example 1 (Python) · videos

Code example 1 (Python) — Network-architecture risk factors of Kalmia

Code example — task

A Python script that reads the four lab files, runs the four checks of Lesson 1 in order — segmentation, exposed services, remote access, wireless — prints every decision with its evidence, and writes network_risk_factors.csv (24 rows). The visualization draws Kalmia's network and shows, while the script runs, the reach lines from untrusted devices to the critical assets, the exposed services and the remote paths.

How it relates to the lecture

It reproduces the reasoning of Lesson 1 step by step: the zone composition decides whether the network is flat, the reachability lines are lateral movement made visible, and each remote path is judged on MFA (multi-factor authentication), end date and logging. Its output is the network part of the Class 9 workshop and of Lab 3.

Execution window — every executed step is kept here; pause and scroll to discuss
    Step by step — what the code does
    1. The script defines the rules of the lesson as data: the device families to separate (OT [operational technology], camera, IoT [Internet of Things], personal, printer), the families to protect (server, workstation, POS [point of sale]), the clear-text administration ports (23, 80, 5000), the remote-control ports (3389, 22), the file-sharing ports (139, 445) and the three critical assets of the Lab 1 business impact analysis.
    2. read_rows() opens each CSV (comma-separated values) file with the csv module and returns one dictionary per row; ports_of() turns a cell such as “23/telnet;80/http” into the list of port numbers.
    3. Check 1 — segmentation: for each internal zone, the script lists the device families present. A zone that mixes families to separate with families to protect and has no internal filtering is recorded as a flat zone (HIGH when it holds a critical asset). Then, for each untrusted device, it prints the critical assets it can reach and their open ports — the REACH lines.
    4. Check 2 — exposed services: Internet hosts offering administration (SSH [Secure Shell], the firewall portal) are HIGH; internal clear-text administration is one finding per host, HIGH when the device still has its factory password; RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) and SMB (Server Message Block) on workstations are MEDIUM.
    5. Check 3 — remote access: each declared flow is tested for MFA (multi-factor authentication), an end date (for outside parties only) and logging. A control path from the Internet with a missing safeguard is HIGH; an undeclared outbound channel is MEDIUM; expected outbound flows are printed as OK.
    6. Check 4 — wireless: a radio not in the inventory is a rogue (HIGH); a shared WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) key older than 365 days is HIGH when bridged into HQ-LAN; WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) on an inventoried router is LOW; a guest network with client isolation is printed as a strength.
    7. The output step writes network_risk_factors.csv and prints the summary: 24 risk factors — HIGH 8, MEDIUM 15, LOW 1.     Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal the answer
    Vulnerability vs risk factorclick to flip
    A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat source could exploit. A risk factor is any input that determines the level of risk — threat, vulnerability, impact, likelihood or predisposing condition — so a vulnerability becomes a risk factor in its context.
    Flat networkclick to flip
    One zone with no internal filtering: every device can reach every port of every other device, so lateral movement needs no special technique. At Kalmia: HQ-LAN, 192.168.10.0/24, internal filtering 'none'.
    Three kinds of exposed servicesclick to flip
    Clear-text administration (Telnet 23, HTTP [Hypertext Transfer Protocol] 80); remote administration reachable from everywhere (RDP [Remote Desktop Protocol] 3389, SSH [Secure Shell] 22); a management interface published on the Internet (CISA [Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency] BOD [Binding Operational Directive] 23-02).
    Four safeguards of a remote-access pathclick to flip
    MFA (multi-factor authentication), an end date or time limit, a record of every session, and a path that reaches only the system to support. RoastLink on ROAST-PC has none of them demonstrated.
    WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with a pre-shared key) weaknessesclick to flip
    One shared password: it can be tested offline after one captured handshake, and it remains valid for everyone who ever knew it, including former employees. WPA3-SAE (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) or 802.1X (IEEE port-based network access control standard) with individual accounts reduce both problems.

    FORMATIVE — not evaluated. Practice only; Quiz 2 is administered separately.
    Question 1. In the language of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1, how should Kalmia's flat head-office network be classified? Multiple choice — one answer
    • ✔ Correct. A predisposing condition is a property of the organization or its architecture that increases the likelihood that a threat event causes harm. The flat network makes every device's weakness more dangerous.
    • ✘ A threat source is the actor or event that could cause harm (a cybercriminal, a fire). The network design does not act by itself.
    • ✘ Impact is the harm that results (stopped production, disclosed data). The flat network is a condition that makes the harm more likely.
    • ✘ A false positive is a reported weakness that does not exist. The flat network is confirmed by the zone table and the scan.
    Hint: It is not a flaw in any single product; it is a property of the design that changes the likelihood of harm.
    Question 2. A port scan of FW-HQ's public address shows no inbound port for RoastLink, yet RoastTech can take control of ROAST-PC from the Internet. What explains this? Multiple choice — one answer
    • ✔ Correct. Remote-support agents start the connection from the inside, so no inbound port is needed. The evidence comes from the contract, the installed software and the outgoing traffic — not from an inbound port scan.
    • ✘ A false positive is a reported weakness that does not exist; here the scan reported nothing, and the access path does exist.
    • ✘ Nothing in the evidence shows Telnet on ROAST-PC; the flow F-06 is an HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) relay on 443/tcp outbound.
    • ✘ Deny by default would block unrequested inbound connections, but it does not stop a connection that the inside device opens itself.
    Hint: Think about which side starts the connection of a remote-support agent.
    Question 3. Which Kalmia finding is a management interface exposed to the Internet, the case targeted by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 23-02? Multiple choice — one answer
    • ✔ Correct. It is the login page that administers the firewall. Until the rule export shows that only InfoNord's address can reach it, it is recorded as exposed (NA-16).
    • ✘ Port 443 of the web shop is the public service customers use; it is supposed to be on the Internet. Its SSH (Secure Shell) port 22 is the administration finding.
    • ✘ The guest network is isolated from the staff network; it is a strength, not an exposed management interface.
    • ✘ SMB (Server Message Block) on a workstation is an internal exposed service, reachable from the flat network, not from the Internet.
    Hint: Look for a device administration page reachable from any public address.
    Question 4. Why is the WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) password of Kalmia-HQ, unchanged since March 15, 2022, rated HIGH and not LOW? Multiple choice — one answer
    • ✔ Correct. A shared key stays valid for everyone who ever knew it (no offboarding, W-06), and once connected, a device is inside HQ-LAN with no internal filtering.
    • ✘ WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) with a long, regularly changed password is acceptable for a small site; WEP and the original WPA are the broken ones.
    • ✘ WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) does not send the password itself; the weakness is offline guessing after a captured handshake and the age of the shared key.
    • ✘ The survey shows WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) off on the two Kalmia access points; WPS is on for the extender and the café router.
    Hint: Combine the age of a shared password with where the Wi-Fi leads.
    Question 5. Which three safeguards does Code example 1 check on every remote-access path? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
    • ✔ Checked: 'mfa' must be 'yes'.
    • ✔ Checked: a vendor or MSP (managed service provider) access without an end date is standing access.
    • ✔ Checked: 'logged' must be 'yes' so that sessions can be reconstructed.
    • ✘ Important, but not a column of the flow table; RoastLink and the portal already use HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure).
    • ✘ Endpoint protection is a different control; the script judges the access path.
    • ✘ Never: scanning a third party's network without written authorization is prohibited (Legal Notice, sections 6.3 and 7.6).
    Hint: Three are checked by the script; the other options are useful controls, but not the ones tested.
    Question 6. Which three Kalmia observations are wireless weaknesses identified in Lesson 1? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
    • ✔ A rogue access point (NA-22).
    • ✔ An insecure default of many ISP (Internet service provider) routers (NA-24).
    • ✔ A stale shared key that former employees may know (NA-21).
    • ✘ This is a control that works; it is recorded as a strength.
    • ✘ An exposed clear-text administration service, not a wireless weakness.
    • ✘ An exposed remote-control service on a workstation, family 'exposed services'.
    Hint: Choose the radio-related findings; one option is a strength, and two belong to other families.

    Lesson 2 — Vulnerable and obsolete applications, operating systems and services
    End-of-support software, missing patches and default configurations — and the evidence that proves each one
    0:24 – 0:42
    ▣ Slide 23 — Vulnerable and obsolete applications, operating systems and services
    Read-aloud script — 12 minutes
    ▣ Slide 24 — Every program has an end date
    Every program has an end date
    Software is not finished when it is sold. The vendor keeps correcting it for a period called support, and that period ends. The software lifecycle is the sequence of phases from release to retirement. Many vendors divide support into mainstream support, with new features and fixes, and extended support, with security fixes only. After the end of support (EOS [end of support]) — many vendors and scanners say end of life (EOL [end of life]), and some reserve EOL for the end of sales, so always read the vendor's definition — the vendor no longer publishes security updates for that product.
    Why is an unsupported product a vulnerability even when no known flaw is open today? Because every flaw discovered after the end date stays open for good. Worse, when the vendor fixes a flaw in the versions it still supports, the published fix shows attackers where to look in the versions it no longer supports. An obsolete product is one that no longer receives fixes or no longer meets current security requirements. The MITRE weakness list has a category for it: CWE-1104, use of unmaintained third-party components.
    ▣ Slide 25 — One product, several clocks
    One product can have several clocks. Windows 10 support ended on October 14, 2025. A program called ESU (Extended Security Updates), Extended Security Updates, can prolong security updates after that date: for home users until October 12, 2027, and for organizations, for a yearly fee, for up to three years. Windows 11 is supported, but each yearly version has its own end date: version 24H2 of the Home and Pro editions stopped receiving updates on October 13, 2026, while version 25H2 is supported until October 12, 2027 and the Enterprise and Education editions of 24H2 until October 12, 2027. A computer that “runs Windows 11” is therefore not automatically supported: the version and the edition decide.
    The same rule applies to the components of a web application. PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) 8.1 reached its end of life on December 31, 2025. On October 21, 2026, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security published alert AL26-026 about two critical PHP vulnerabilities and listed the fixed releases — for supported branches only. A web shop that runs PHP 8.1 cannot install that fix, because it does not exist for its branch.
    ▣ Slide 26 — Kalmia — what has ended, or ends soon
    Now Kalmia. Lucas Martin's software inventory from Lab 1 shows three computers on Windows 10: ROAST-PC and the two sales laptops. Kalmia has not enrolled them in the ESU (Extended Security Updates) program, so all three are past their end of support and receive no security updates. Two warehouse computers, PC-SHIP-01 and PC-WH-01, still run Windows 11 Pro 24H2: their last updates were downloaded in July and August, but they were never restarted, and their version ended on October 13. The web shop's hosting panel is set to PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) 8.1.27. And the roaster software RoastMaster 4.2, which runs on ROAST-PC, is supported by its vendor until March 31, 2027 — 145 days from tonight. That last case is called end of support soon: nothing is broken yet, but the replacement must be planned now, because an OT (operational technology) change needs the vendor, a maintenance window and a test of the roaster.
    ROAST-PC shows a problem that is typical of operational technology. RoastTech certifies one exact configuration of Windows and forbids updates that it has not tested, so the computer's last update dates from March 12, 2024. The vendor's rule does not remove the vulnerability; it explains why the usual remedy is not available, and it moves the discussion to compensating controls — isolation, controlled vendor access, monitoring — which Topics 6 and 7 will cover.
    ▣ Slide 27 — Missing patches — the vocabulary
    Missing patches
    A patch is a change to a program, published by its vendor, that corrects a defect or a vulnerability. A security update is a patch whose purpose is security; Microsoft packages its monthly fixes into one cumulative update, released on Patch Tuesday, the second Tuesday of every month — October 13, 2026 was the last one, and the next is November 10. An out-of-band update is published outside that schedule when a flaw is too urgent to wait.
    ▣ Slide 28 — Patch management and the patch gap
    NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-40 Rev. 4 defines enterprise patch management as the process of identifying, prioritizing, acquiring, installing and verifying the installation of patches, updates and upgrades throughout an organization. Each verb matters. Identifying needs an inventory. Verifying means checking that the patch is really active — an update that waits for a restart protects nothing. The time between the publication of a fix and its installation is the patch gap. Kalmia's draft policy, proposed by InfoNord, allows 30 days for security updates; Lab 4 will decide whether that is enough.
    Time matters because public fixes are studied by attackers as quickly as by defenders. The PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) alert of October 21 first reported a public proof of concept and no exploitation; five days later the Cyber Centre updated it to report exploitation in the wild, and CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue. A patch gap of 30 days would have left a vulnerable web shop exposed for most of that period.
    ▣ Slide 29 — Firmware, applications, plugins — Kalmia's pattern
    Patches are not only for Windows. Firmware — the software inside a camera, a printer, a switch, a firewall or a storage appliance — receives fixes too, but nobody installs them unless someone owns the task. Applications installed by users, browser extensions and web-site plugins are updated separately from the operating system. At Kalmia, the evidence shows the pattern clearly: the office PCs (personal computers) and Microsoft 365 Apps are updated automatically and are current; everything that depends on a person is behind. NAS-01's automatic updates were turned off and its last update dates from May 2024. The cameras CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4 still run the firmware installed in June 2019. The printer's firmware dates from February 2021. On the web shop, the backup plugin UpdraftPlus is still at version 1.26.4, although version 1.26.5, published in June 2026, fixes CVE-2026-10795, an authentication bypass rated 8.1 by NVD (National Vulnerability Database).
    ▣ Slide 30 — Default configurations
    Default configurations
    The default configuration is the set of settings a product has when it leaves the box. Vendors choose defaults that make installation easy, not settings that make the product safe. The most dangerous defaults are default credentials — a factory user name and password printed in the manual and therefore known to everyone — and services enabled by default that the buyer does not need: Telnet, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) with the community name “public”, UPnP (Universal Plug and Play), which lets devices open ports in the router on their own, and WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup). MITRE classifies this weakness as CWE-1188, initialization of a resource with an insecure default.
    The danger is not theoretical. In 2016 the Mirai botnet took control of hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers simply by trying their factory passwords, then used them to flood major Internet services. CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) lists the use of known or default passwords among its bad practices and asks manufacturers to stop shipping products with shared default passwords at all.
    ▣ Slide 31 — Hardening — and Kalmia's seven insecure configurations
    The remedy is hardening: changing the defaults to reduce the attack surface — new passwords, unnecessary services disabled, encrypted administration only. Organizations harden against a written configuration baseline, often derived from the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks, and compare devices with it regularly, because settings drift over time. At Kalmia the walk-through and the scan found seven default or insecure configurations: the cameras CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4 with factory passwords and Telnet on; the printer answering to “public” with an administration page and no password; the extender EXT-WH-01 accepting admin/admin with WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) on; NAS-01 with its built-in admin account enabled and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) administration on port 5000; the café router with the administration password from its label, WPS and UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) on; and one manager PIN (personal identification number) shared by all the shift leads of each café.
    ▣ Slide 32 — An exhaustive method — and why 'unknown' is a finding
    An exhaustive method, and why 'unknown' is a finding
    Criterion 3.2 asks for an exhaustive identification. Exhaustive does not mean that you test everything by hand; it means that you start from the complete software inventory of Lab 1 and give every row a status, with a source. For each product you record the version, the vendor's end-of-support date and the page where you read it, the date of the last update and how updates are installed — automatically, manually, by a vendor, by the MSP (managed service provider) or by nobody — and the default settings still in place. The status is one of: supported, end of support soon, end of support, patch gap, insecure configuration, or unknown.
    Unknown is not a blank cell; it is a finding. At Kalmia, nobody can say today when the firmware of FW-HQ was last updated, whether the vendor still supports the camera firmware, or which firmware runs on the café router. Each unknown becomes a question with an owner: InfoNord for the firewall, the ISP (Internet service provider) for the router, Lucas Martin for the cameras once Lesson 3's scan has identified their model. Code example 2 applies this method to the 18 rows of Kalmia's software inventory and finds 34 problems: 6 end of support, 1 end of support soon, 10 patch gaps, 7 insecure configurations and 10 unknowns.
    Key terms to learn
    software lifecycle
    the phases of a product from release to retirement (mainstream support, extended support, end of support)
    end of support (EOS [end of support]) / end of life (EOL [end of life])
    the date after which the vendor publishes no more security updates (read each vendor's definition)
    end of support soon
    support still runs but ends within the planning window (180 days in Code example 2)
    Extended Security Updates (ESU [Extended Security Updates])
    a paid program that prolongs security updates after the end of support (Windows 10)
    obsolete software
    software that no longer receives fixes or no longer meets current security requirements (CWE-1104)
    patch / security update / cumulative update
    a vendor change that corrects a defect / a patch for security / one package containing all previous fixes
    Patch Tuesday / out-of-band update
    Microsoft's monthly release (second Tuesday) / an urgent update published outside the schedule
    enterprise patch management
    identifying, prioritizing, acquiring, installing and verifying patches throughout an organization (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-40 Rev. 4)
    patch gap
    the time between the publication of a fix and its installation
    firmware
    the software inside a device such as a camera, printer, switch, firewall or storage appliance
    default configuration / default credentials
    the factory settings / the factory user name and password, known from the manual
    insecure default
    a factory setting that weakens security (CWE-1188): Telnet on, SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) 'public', UPnP (Universal Plug and Play) on, WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) on
    hardening
    changing settings to reduce the attack surface: new passwords, unused services disabled, encrypted administration
    configuration baseline
    the written set of secure settings a device must match (often based on CIS [Center for Internet Security] Benchmarks)
    compensating control
    a measure that reduces a risk when the normal remedy is not possible (for example, isolating an unpatchable OT [operational technology] computer)

    ▣ Slide 36 — Code example 2 (Bash) · videos
    Code example 2 (Bash) — Software lifecycle and patch-gap audit of Kalmia
    Code example — task
    A Bash script that loads the vendor lifecycle table into an associative array, reads the 18 rows of the software inventory, and applies three tests to each row — lifecycle, patch gap, configuration — printing a tagged line (EOL [end of life], EOL-SOON, PATCH-GAP, CONFIG, UNKNOWN, OK, INFO) and writing software_findings.csv. The visualization draws, while the script runs, the support timeline of each product against today's date, the patch-age bars against the 30-day policy, and the configuration flags.
    How it relates to the lecture
    It is the exhaustive method of Lesson 2 in executable form: every inventory row receives a status with its source, an unknown date is recorded as a finding, and an ended product whose final update is installed is explained instead of being reported twice. The execution window shows Bash's own trace (set -x), so every comparison of dates can be read with its real values.
    kalmia_lifecycle_audit.sh
    Step 0 /  · line – · the highlighted line has just been executed
    Variables changed by this step
    Program output
    Visualization — updates while the code runs 
    Execution window — every executed step is kept here; pause and scroll to discuss
      Step by step — what the code does
      1. set -euo pipefail makes the script stop on the first error. TODAY is fixed to 2026-11-06 and converted to seconds with date -u, so every student gets the same numbers and a daylight-saving change cannot shift a result by one day.
      2. The policy values are declared: 30 days for security updates and a 180-day planning window for products whose support ends soon.
      3. declare -A creates two associative arrays, EOS (end of support) and SRC. The while-read loop reads lifecycle.csv (minus its header, through tail -n +2) and stores, for every product key, the end-of-support date and its source.
      4. record() is a function that numbers each finding (SW-01, SW-02 …), prints it with its tag and appends it to software_findings.csv.
      5. The main loop reads software_inventory.csv, one row at a time, into nine variables. Test 1 looks up the end-of-support date: 'unknown' → UNKNOWN; 'active' → maintained continuously; a date → the days left are computed as (end − today) / 86,400 seconds, giving EOL (end of life) when negative and EOL-SOON when 180 days or fewer remain.
      6. Test 2 computes the age of the last update. An unknown date is UNKNOWN; for a product whose support has ended and whose final update is installed, the script prints INFO instead of a patch gap; otherwise an age above 30 days is a PATCH-GAP, with the update mode that explains it (vendor-only, restart pending, auto-update off, none).
      7. Test 3 records any default or insecure configuration as CONFIG. The summary line prints 34 findings: EOL (end of life) 6, EOL-SOON 1, PATCH-GAP 10, CONFIG 7, UNKNOWN 10. In the runner, each step shows the line number and the command exactly as Bash expanded it, for example left=-388.
      Run it yourself in Hours 2–3: download the lab files below the Reference tables, put them in one folder with the script, and run bash kalmia_lifecycle_audit.sh. Fictional lab data only (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 7.5).

      Five flash-cards — click a card to reveal the answer
      End of support (EOS [end of support]) and why it mattersclick to flip
      The date after which the vendor stops publishing security updates. Every flaw found later stays open, and fixes published for supported versions show attackers where to look in the unsupported one.
      Windows: one product, several clocksclick to flip
      Windows 10 ended October 14, 2025; only ESU (Extended Security Updates) enrolment (paid for organizations) extends security updates. Windows 11 Home/Pro 24H2 ended October 13, 2026; 25H2 runs to October 12, 2027. The version and the edition decide.
      Enterprise patch management (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-40 Rev. 4)click to flip
      Identifying, prioritizing, acquiring, installing and verifying the installation of patches, updates and upgrades throughout an organization. An update waiting for a restart is not installed.
      Default credentials and insecure defaultsclick to flip
      Factory user names and passwords known from the manual, and services enabled out of the box (Telnet, SNMP [Simple Network Management Protocol] 'public', UPnP [Universal Plug and Play], WPS [Wi-Fi Protected Setup]). Mirai (2016) took over IoT (Internet of Things) devices with factory passwords. CWE-1188.
      Why 'unknown' is a findingclick to flip
      An exhaustive identification gives every inventory row a status with a source. An unknown end date or update date is a question with an owner (MSP [managed service provider], ISP [Internet service provider], vendor) — hiding it gives a false sense of security.
      Formative quiz — 4 multiple-choice + 2 multiple-select questions
      FORMATIVE — not evaluated. Practice only; Quiz 2 is administered separately.
      Question 1. On November 6, 2026, PC-SHIP-01 runs Windows 11 Pro version 24H2. What is its support status? Multiple choice — one answer
      • ✔ Correct. The edition (Pro) and the version (24H2) decide. Installing 25H2 (supported to October 12, 2027) and restarting brings it back into support.
      • ✘ This is the common trap: 'Windows 11' is not one date. 24H2 Home/Pro ended on October 13, 2026.
      • ✘ That is the date for 24H2 Enterprise and Education editions, and for 25H2 Home/Pro — not for 24H2 Pro.
      • ✘ ESU (Extended Security Updates) is a Windows 10 program; it does not apply to Windows 11 versions.
      Hint: Windows 11 is supported, but each yearly version of each edition has its own end date.
      Question 2. RoastTech forbids updates on ROAST-PC, whose last update dates from March 12, 2024. How should the analyst record this? Multiple choice — one answer
      • ✔ Correct. The vendor rule explains why patching is not possible; it moves the treatment to isolation, controlled vendor access and monitoring (Topics 6 and 7).
      • ✘ Responsibility does not remove the weakness, and the risk stays with Kalmia, which owns the roaster and its data.
      • ✘ A false positive is a reported weakness that does not exist. The unsupported OS (operating system) and the missing updates are real.
      • ✘ The facts are known: Windows 10, last update March 12, 2024, vendor-only update mode.
      Hint: A rule that prevents the remedy does not remove the weakness.
      Question 3. Which statement matches the definition of enterprise patch management in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-40 Rev. 4? Multiple choice — one answer
      • ✔ Correct. 'Verifying' is why PC-SHIP-01 and PC-WH-01, whose updates wait for a restart, are recorded as patch gaps.
      • ✘ Speed matters, but the definition is a process that also identifies, prioritizes and verifies.
      • ✘ Replacement is one possible treatment; patch management concerns supported products.
      • ✘ Automatic updates help, but firmware, plugins and OT (operational technology) systems need other steps, and installation must still be verified.
      Hint: The definition contains five verbs, and the last one checks the result.
      Question 4. Why can the web shop not install the fix listed in Cyber Centre alert AL26-026? Multiple choice — one answer
      • ✔ Correct. The remedy is to move to a supported branch (8.3 or later) after testing the plugins — an upgrade, not a patch.
      • ✘ The Cyber Centre publishes alerts; fixes come from the PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) project and are installed by the host or the site owner.
      • ✘ WordPress does not block PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) updates; the PHP version is chosen in the hosting panel.
      • ✘ That is true of a different flaw (CVE-2024-4577, PHP-CGI on Windows) that appears as a false positive in Lesson 3 — not of AL26-026.
      Hint: Look at the PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) branch the hosting panel uses and at its end date.
      Question 5. Which three items are insecure default configurations found at Kalmia? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
      • ✔ Default credentials (W-07).
      • ✔ A default community string that discloses the device's configuration.
      • ✔ Default credentials and an insecure default service.
      • ✘ That is a patch gap (an update not yet active), not a default configuration.
      • ✘ That is 'end of support soon', a lifecycle status.
      • ✘ That is an end-of-support finding, not a configuration.
      Hint: Default = the setting the device had when it left the box.
      Question 6. Which three rows does Code example 2 record as UNKNOWN? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
      • ✔ To be requested from InfoNord, which manages the firewall.
      • ✔ To be requested from the ISP (Internet service provider).
      • ✔ The model must be confirmed first (Lesson 3's scan identifies it).
      • ✘ Known: October 14, 2025 — recorded as EOL (end of life).
      • ✘ Known: October 14, 2026 — within the 30-day policy.
      • ✘ Known: 1.26.4 — recorded as a patch gap.
      Hint: UNKNOWN means a date that nobody can document today, not a bad result.

      Lesson 3 — Reading and interpreting a vulnerability scan report
      What a scanner does, the anatomy of a report and a finding, CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), false positives, and the seven-step reading method
      0:42 – 0:58
      ▣ Slide 37 — Reading and interpreting a vulnerability scan report
      Read-aloud script — 11 minutes
      ▣ Slide 38 — What a vulnerability scanner does
      What a vulnerability scanner does — and what it does not do
      A vulnerability scanner is a program that discovers the hosts and services of a network, identifies the software and versions behind them, reads their configuration where it can, and compares everything with a database of known vulnerabilities. Each comparison is a small test, called a plugin by some products and an NVT (Network Vulnerability Test) by Greenbone, the company behind the open-source scanner OpenVAS. Commercial products such as Tenable Nessus work the same way.
      A scan is a vulnerability assessment: it identifies weaknesses that probably exist, without exploiting them. A penetration test goes further and tries to exploit them to prove the impact. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-115 makes the same distinction between identifying vulnerabilities and validating them. That difference explains most of what follows tonight: a scanner draws conclusions from versions, banners and settings, and conclusions can be wrong.
      There are two kinds of scans. An unauthenticated scan looks at the host from the network, like an outsider: it sees open ports, banners and the answers of services. An authenticated scan, also called a credentialed scan, logs in to the host with an account and reads the installed packages, the patch level and the configuration directly. The authenticated scan is far more accurate — it finds missing patches that no banner shows and avoids many wrong conclusions — but it needs an account, which is why section 7.6 of the Legal Notice requires written authorization for it.
      ▣ Slide 39 — Two rules before you open any report
      Two legal points before you open any report. Scanning is an intrusive act: in this course it is done only on the designated targets of the lab range, never on a network you do not control — not the college's, not an employer's, not a café's Wi-Fi. And a scan report is a confidential finding under section 7.5: it is a precise map of how to attack the organization. It is stored with care, shared only with those who need it, and never uploaded to a public service.
      ▣ Slide 40 — Anatomy of a report — read the header first
      The anatomy of a scan report
      Every report, whatever the product, has the same parts. The header says who ran the scan, when, with which scanner and which database date, on which targets, with which exclusions and credentials, and how many hosts answered. The summary counts the results by severity and by host. The detailed results follow, host by host. Read the header first: a report without a date, a scope and an authorization cannot be used as evidence.
      The Kalmia report was produced on November 4 by InfoNord with Greenbone, with the written authorization of Nadia Roy signed on November 2. Its scope is the head-office network, the public address of FW-HQ and the web shop server, whose host's testing policy was checked first. Two details in the header change how you read everything else. ROAST-PC was excluded at the vendor's request, and the laptop SALES-LT2 did not answer because it was on the road. Neither appears in the results — which does not mean that either is safe. That is a false negative risk: a weakness that exists but is not reported.
      ▣ Slide 41 — The fields of a finding
      Each finding, or result, has the same fields: the name of the problem; the host and port where it was found; the severity, expressed as a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score with its vector; the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) identifiers when the problem is a known vulnerability; the QoD (Quality of Detection), Greenbone's Quality of Detection, a percentage that says how sure the scanner is; the evidence, that is, what the scanner actually saw — a version number, a banner, a successful login; and the solution, with references to the vendor's advisory. The evidence field is the one beginners skip and professionals read first.
      ▣ Slide 42 — Reading severity — CVSS ratings and the vector
      Reading severity: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)
      The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, maintained by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), gives every vulnerability a base score from 0.0 to 10.0 and a qualitative rating: None for 0.0 — shown as Log or Info in scanners — Low from 0.1 to 3.9, Medium from 4.0 to 6.9, High from 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical from 9.0 to 10.0. Version 4.0, published in November 2023, keeps the same ranges; many tools still display version 3.1, as the Kalmia report does.
      The score is calculated from a vector, a short text that you can read. Take CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System):3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. AV:N means the attacker can act from the network; AC:L, attack complexity low; PR:N, no privileges required; UI:N, no user interaction; S:U, the scope is unchanged; C:H/I:H/A:H, high impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. That vector gives 9.8, Critical. Change AC to H — the attacker needs conditions he does not control — and the same vector gives 8.1, High.
      ▣ Slide 43 — Severity is not priority
      Now the most important sentence of this lesson: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) measures severity, not risk. The base score describes the flaw in general, in any organization. The priority of a finding for Kalmia also depends on evidence of exploitation, on exposure and on the asset. Two public sources give the exploitation evidence. The KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) lists vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild. EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), published daily by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams), estimates the probability that exploitation activity for a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be observed in the next 30 days. The asset side comes from your own Lab 1: is the host on the Internet, and how critical is it to the business? CISA also publishes a decision method, SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization), that combines these questions into four decisions: track, track closely, attend or act.
      ▣ Slide 44 — False positives — two in the Kalmia report
      Interpreting: false positives, false negatives, duplicates and noise
      A false positive is a reported vulnerability that does not exist on that host. The Kalmia report has two, and they are instructive. Result R04 reports CVE-2024-4577, rated 9.8 and listed in KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities), on the web shop: the scanner read PHP/8.1.27 in a web header and compared the number with the affected versions. But that flaw concerns PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) running as CGI on Windows, and the web shop runs Linux. Result R05 reports CVE-2024-6387, the OpenSSH flaw called regreSSHion, because the banner says OpenSSH 8.9p1; but Ubuntu applied the fix to its package without changing the upstream version number — a backport — and the full banner shows the fixed package, 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10. Both results are removed, and the reason is written down so that the decision can be checked later.
      ▣ Slide 45 — Noise: Log results, low QoD, duplicates
      Three other kinds of results must be handled before ranking. Informational results, with severity 0.0, are not vulnerabilities: open ports, the operating system detected, a host that did not answer. They are useful to check your inventory. Results with a low QoD (Quality of Detection) — Greenbone hides those below 70 % by default — are guesses that a person must verify; at Kalmia, result R17 suspects default credentials on the switch from a login prompt, without trying to log in. And duplicates are one problem found on several hosts: SMB (Server Message Block) signing not required appears on NAS-01, PC-FIN-01 and PC-IT-01, but it is one remediation action. Count actions, not lines.
      ▣ Slide 46 — The seven-step reading method
      The seven-step reading method
      Put together, the method has seven steps. One: check the scope — date, targets, exclusions, credentials, hosts alive. Two: convert every score into its rating. Three: set aside informational results and low-QoD results to verify. Four: verify suspicious results and remove false positives with a written reason. Five: group the results that need the same action. Six: prioritize — in this course with a transparent teaching rule: the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score, plus 3 if the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is in KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities), plus 1 if EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) is 0.10 or more, plus 2 if the host is reachable from the Internet, plus the criticality of the asset from 1 to 3. A total of 14 or more is P1, fixed within 7 days; 11 or more is P2, 30 days; 8 or more is P3, 90 days; below 8 is P4. Seven: record each action as a row with its evidence.
      ▣ Slide 47 — Kalmia: 27 results → 16 actions
      Applied to Kalmia, the method turns 27 results into 16 actions. Two are P1: the web shop's PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) 8.1, past its end of life on an Internet-facing server that brings in a quarter of the revenue, and the two cameras vulnerable to CVE-2017-7921, an authentication flaw published in 2017 and added to the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue in March 2026 — a reminder that old flaws in forgotten devices are still used. Notice what the method removed: the highest-scoring line of the raw report, R04, would have totalled 18.8 — and it was a false positive. A report read from the top down sends the team to fix a problem that does not exist.
      Finally, compare the scanner's view with the architecture view of Lesson 1. The scanner rated the firewall's administration portal only through its weak encryption settings — SWEET32 and old TLS (Transport Layer Security) versions, P2 and P3. It reported the portal itself as information. Lesson 1 rated the same portal HIGH because it is a management interface on the Internet. Neither view is complete alone. That is why Lab 3 combines the NA-, SW- and VS- rows into one risk register.
      Key terms to learn
      vulnerability scanner
      a program that discovers hosts and services, identifies software and settings, and compares them with a database of known vulnerabilities
      plugin / NVT (Network Vulnerability Test)
      one test of the scanner (Greenbone calls it a Network Vulnerability Test)
      vulnerability assessment vs penetration test
      identifying probable weaknesses without exploiting them / trying to exploit them to prove the impact (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-115)
      unauthenticated vs authenticated scan
      a view from the network / a scan that logs in and reads packages, patches and settings directly
      scope / exclusion
      the targets the scan was authorized to test / a target deliberately left out (ROAST-PC)
      finding (result)
      one reported problem: name, host and port, severity, CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) vector, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures), QoD (Quality of Detection), evidence, solution
      CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) base score and vector
      a 0.0–10.0 severity calculated from metrics written as a vector (AV, AC, PR, UI, S, C, I, A)
      severity vs priority
      how serious a flaw is in general / how urgently this organization must fix it
      KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities)
      CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)'s catalogue of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild
      EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System)
      FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams)'s daily probability that exploitation activity for a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be observed in the next 30 days
      Quality of Detection (QoD [Quality of Detection])
      Greenbone's percentage of confidence in a result; results below 70 % are hidden by default
      false positive / false negative
      a reported weakness that does not exist / an existing weakness that is not reported
      backport
      a fix applied by a distribution to an older version without changing its version number
      informational result (Log)
      a 0.0 result that describes the host (ports, OS [operating system]) and is not a vulnerability
      remediation action
      one task that fixes a problem, possibly on several hosts (grouping duplicates)
      SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization)
      CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency)'s decision tree that ranks vulnerabilities into track, track closely, attend or act

      ▣ Slide 51 — Code example 3 (Python) · videos
      Code example 3 (Python) — Triage of the Kalmia scan report
      Code example — task
      A Python script that applies the seven-step reading method to the CSV (comma-separated values) export of the scan: it prints the scope and the coverage gaps, rates every result, sets aside Log and low-QoD results, removes the false positives listed in the analyst's verification file, groups the remaining results into actions, computes the priority score with its detail, and writes scan_risk_factors.csv. The visualization builds, while the script runs, the severity histogram of the raw report and the ranked list of actions with their priority class.
      How it relates to the lecture
      It makes every decision of Lesson 3 explicit and checkable: the CVSS-to-rating rule, the QoD (Quality of Detection) threshold, the written reason for each false positive, the grouping of duplicates and the arithmetic of the priority score. Its output is the scan part of the Lab 3 risk register.
      kalmia_scan_triage.py
      Step 0 /  · line – · the highlighted line has just been executed
      Variables changed by this step
      Program output
      Visualization — updates while the code runs 
      Execution window — every executed step is kept here; pause and scroll to discuss
        Step by step — what the code does
        1. severity() converts a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) base score into FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams)'s qualitative rating; 0.0 is shown as 'Log', as scanners do.
        2. Step 1 reads scan_meta.txt (the report header) into a dictionary and prints the date, authorization, scope, exclusion, credentials and hosts alive. When fewer hosts answered than were targeted, a COVERAGE line records the gap: no findings does not mean no weakness.
        3. Step 2 reads the 27 results, the asset criticality table and the verification notes. Each result receives its numeric score and its rating, is printed as a RAW line, and the counts by rating are printed like the report's summary.
        4. Steps 3 and 4 filter: Log results are printed as INFO; results with QoD (Quality of Detection) below 70 are printed as VERIFY; results that the analyst marked as false positives are printed as FP with the reason and removed; confirmed results are printed as CONFIRMED.
        5. Step 5 groups the 20 remaining results by title with dict.setdefault(): one title = one remediation action, possibly on several hosts — 16 actions.
        6. Step 6 computes, for each action, the highest CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), +3 for KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities), +1 for EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) ≥ 0.10, +2 for an Internet-facing host and the criticality of the most important host, then finds the priority class (P1 ≥ 14, P2 ≥ 11, P3 ≥ 8, otherwise P4) and the due date. The actions are sorted by score and printed with the full calculation.
        7. Step 7 writes scan_risk_factors.csv with the result numbers as evidence and prints the summary: 27 results read → 16 actions (P1 2, P2 6, P3 7, P4 1). In the runner, Next output jumps from one printed line to the next, which is the fastest way to follow the seven steps in class.

        Vulnerability assessment vs penetration testclick to flip
        A scan identifies probable weaknesses from versions, banners and settings without exploiting them; a penetration test tries to exploit them to prove the impact (NIST [National Institute of Standards and Technology] SP [Special Publication] 800-115).
        Authenticated scanclick to flip
        The scanner logs in and reads installed packages, patch levels and settings directly. More accurate than an unauthenticated scan; needs written authorization (Legal Notice, s. 7.6, Annex D).
        CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) ratingsclick to flip
        None 0.0 (Log) · Low 0.1–3.9 · Medium 4.0–6.9 · High 7.0–8.9 · Critical 9.0–10.0. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) measures severity, not risk.
        Two false positives in the Kalmia reportclick to flip
        R04: CVE-2024-4577 is a PHP-CGI flaw on Windows; the web shop runs Linux. R05: CVE-2024-6387 was fixed by Ubuntu in package 1:8.9p1-3ubuntu0.10 (a backport) without changing the version number.
        The seven-step reading methodclick to flip
        Scope → severity → noise (Log, QoD [Quality of Detection] < 70) → verify (false positives) → group (actions) → prioritize (CVSS [Common Vulnerability Scoring System] + KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] + EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System] + exposure + criticality) → record (VS- rows for Lab 3).
        Formative quiz — 4 multiple-choice + 2 multiple-select questions
        FORMATIVE — not evaluated. Practice only; Quiz 2 is administered separately.
        Question 1. What is the main difference between an authenticated and an unauthenticated vulnerability scan? Multiple choice — one answer
        • ✔ Correct. It finds missing patches that no banner shows and avoids many false positives. It needs an account and, in this course, written authorization (s. 7.6).
        • ✘ Neither kind exploits vulnerabilities; exploitation is the work of a penetration test.
        • ✘ No. Any scan, and a credentialed one even more, needs authorization and an approved scope.
        • ✘ CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) scores come from the scanner's database and the NVD (National Vulnerability Database), not from the host.
        Hint: Think about what the scanner can see when it has an account on the host.
        Question 2. Result R03 (PHP [PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor] end-of-life detection) is shown with the vector CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System):3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. What does S:C mean, and what is the rating? Multiple choice — one answer
        • ✔ Correct. A changed scope with high C/I/A impact and no conditions gives the maximum, 10.0, rated Critical (9.0–10.0).
        • ✘ S is the Scope metric, not a vendor classification.
        • ✘ Scanners do not confirm by exploitation, and 10.0 is Critical, not High.
        • ✘ The base score is calculated by the scoring authority from the vector; 10.0 is Critical.
        Hint: S is the Scope metric; the score is 10.0.
        Question 3. Why is R05 (OpenSSH regreSSHion, CVE-2024-6387) a false positive on SHOP-VPS? Multiple choice — one answer
        • ✔ Correct. A banner-based check compares 8.9p1 with the affected range and ignores the distribution's patch level. An authenticated check of the package would not report it.
        • ✘ That explains R04 (PHP-CGI on Windows), not R05.
        • ✘ OpenSSH is installed; port 22 answers with its banner.
        • ✘ R05 has QoD (Quality of Detection) 80; it passes the filter, which is why it had to be verified.
        Hint: Read the whole banner, not only the upstream version number.
        Question 4. In the course's priority rule, what is the score of the action 'PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) 8.1 end of life' on SHOP-VPS (CVSS [Common Vulnerability Scoring System] 10.0, not in KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities], no EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System], Internet-facing, criticality 3)? Multiple choice — one answer
        • ✔ Correct: 10.0 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 3 = 15.0, which is 14 or more (P1, due November 13).
        • ✘ That is only the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score; exposure and criticality must be added.
        • ✘ KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (+3) does not apply: an end-of-life detection has no CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) in KEV.
        • ✘ The criticality of the web shop is 3, not 0: 10 + 2 + 3 = 15.
        Hint: Score = CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) + 3 (KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities]) + 1 (EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System] ≥ 0.10) + 2 (Internet) + criticality.
        Question 5. Which three statements correctly describe information found in the Kalmia report header (step 1)? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
        • ✔ An exclusion: the host was not tested, so its weaknesses must come from other evidence.
        • ✔ A coverage gap: the laptop was off-site.
        • ✔ Required for any scan, and for a credentialed scan in particular (s. 7.6, Annex D).
        • ✘ That is a finding (R09), not header information.
        • ✘ False positives are decided at step 4 by the analyst, not stated in the header.
        • ✘ Never: a scan report is a confidential finding (s. 7.5).
        Hint: The header is about the scan itself, not about any single vulnerability.
        Question 6. Which three results must be set aside or verified before ranking (steps 3 and 4)? Multiple select(3 answers expected)
        • ✔ Below the 70 % threshold: a person must verify it before it can be ranked.
        • ✔ An informational result: it describes coverage, not a vulnerability.
        • ✔ A false positive: the flaw concerns PHP-CGI on Windows.
        • ✘ Confirmed by the firmware page; it is ranked P1.
        • ✘ Confirmed by an authenticated check (QoD [Quality of Detection] 97); it is ranked P2.
        • ✘ Confirmed (QoD [Quality of Detection] 97); it is ranked P2.
        Hint: Look for informational results, low QoD (Quality of Detection) and a claim that does not match the platform.

        22/tcpSSH (Secure Shell) — encrypted remote administrationAdministration interfaces, serversPassword guessing when reachable from the Internet or from every device; default accounts on appliances
        23/tcpTelnet — remote administration in clear textNowhere on a modern networkPasswords travel unencrypted; often enabled by default on cameras and switches
        53/tcp-udpDNS (Domain Name System) — name resolutionFirewall or DNS (Domain Name System) serverA DNS (Domain Name System) service on a Wi-Fi extender or a workstation reveals an unmanaged device
        80/tcpHTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — web without encryptionRedirect to HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) onlyAdministration logins in clear text (switch, cameras, printers, NAS [network-attached storage] on 5000)
        139, 445/tcpNetBIOS session and SMB (Server Message Block) — Windows file sharingFile serversOn workstations it exposes their disks and stored credentials to the whole zone
        161/udpSNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) — device monitoringMonitoring server onlyDefault community 'public' discloses configuration; SNMPv1/v2c is unencrypted
        443/tcpHTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) — encrypted webPublic web services; administration from a management zoneA firewall's administration portal on the Internet (BOD [Binding Operational Directive] 23-02)
        554/tcpRTSP (Real-Time Streaming Protocol) — video streamsCameras, towards the recorderVideo of people is personal information; cameras are rarely patched
        3389/tcpRDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) — Windows remote desktopReachable only from an administration host or through a VPN (virtual private network)One of the most common ransomware entry points when exposed
        5000/tcpHTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) on an alternative port (NAS [network-attached storage] administration)Nowhere; use HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) (5001)Shared NAS (network-attached storage) administrator password sent in clear text
        Network zones (after the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's zoning model)
        ZoneWhat it holdsKalmia todayRule between zones
        Public ZoneThe Internet and everything Kalmia does not controlInternet, ISP (Internet service provider) networks, customersUntrusted: everything that comes in is filtered
        Public Access Zone (comparable to a DMZ [demilitarized zone])Services that must be reachable from the InternetWeb shop (hosted outside); FW-HQ administration portal (should not be there)Only the published service ports; no direct path to internal zones
        Operations ZoneOrdinary workstations and internal serversPCs (personal computers), NAS-01 — but in the same network as everything elseDefault deny from less trusted zones; only required flows
        Restricted / OT (operational technology) zoneProduction systems that must keep runningROAST-PC and LOG-ROAST-01 — not separatedOnly the documented flows (weekly copy to NAS-01; vendor access through a controlled path)
        Device zone (cameras, IoT [Internet of Things], printers)Devices that are rarely patchedCameras, thermostat, printers — not separatedMay reach their recorder or cloud service only
        Guest / BYOD (bring your own device) zoneVisitors' and employees' personal devicesKalmia-Invite in the cafés (isolated); phones on Kalmia-HQ (not isolated)Internet only; no route to any internal zone
        Management zoneAdministration interfaces and the administration workstationDoes not exist: PC-IT-01 administers from the flat networkAdministration ports reachable only from here
        Wi-Fi security modes
        ModeHow a device is admittedMain weaknessVerdict
        Open (no password)Anyone joinsTraffic readable by everyone around unless each site uses HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure)Guest networks only, with isolation
        WEP / WPA (original)Shared keyBroken protocolsNever acceptable
        WPA2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 with a pre-shared key) (Personal)One password shared by everyoneThe password can be tested offline after one handshake capture; it stays valid for people who leftAcceptable only with a long password changed at every departure
        WPA3-SAE (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) (Personal)One password, protected exchangeStill one shared passwordPreferred for small sites
        WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2)/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X [IEEE port-based network access control standard])Individual account checked by a RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) serverNeeds a server and certificatesRecommended for staff networks

        CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) v3.1 base metrics and qualitative ratings
        ItemValuesWhat it means
        AV — Attack VectorN (network) · A (adjacent) · L (local) · P (physical)From where the attacker must act; N is the widest
        AC — Attack ComplexityL (low) · H (high)Conditions beyond the attacker's control that must exist
        PR — Privileges RequiredN (none) · L (low) · H (high)Account level needed before the attack
        UI — User InteractionN (none) · R (required)Whether a user must do something (open, click)
        S — ScopeU (unchanged) · C (changed)Whether the impact reaches components beyond the vulnerable one
        C / I / A — ImpactH (high) · L (low) · N (none)Effect on confidentiality, integrity and availability
        Rating None0.0Scanners show it as Log / Info
        Rating Low0.1 – 3.9
        Rating Medium4.0 – 6.9
        Rating High7.0 – 8.9
        Rating Critical9.0 – 10.0
        Greenbone Quality of Detection (QoD [Quality of Detection]) — how sure the scanner is
        QoD (Quality of Detection)Detection method (examples)How to read it
        100 %The vulnerability was exploited during the testCertain
        97 – 99 %Authenticated package or registry check; remote check of the vulnerable behaviourVery reliable
        95 %Remote active check (for example a login with default credentials succeeded)Reliable
        80 %Version read from a banner or from the product's web pageReliable unless the vendor backports fixes
        70 %Remote analysis of indirect signsDefault threshold of the report view
        30 % or lessUnreliable banner or a general noteHidden by default; must be verified by a person
        The seven-step reading method and Kalmia's priority rule (teaching aid)
        StepWhat you doKalmia example
        1 ScopeRead date, targets, exclusions, credentials, hosts aliveROAST-PC excluded; SALES-LT2 not alive
        2 SeverityConvert every CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score to its rating27 results: 11 Critical, 4 High, 8 Medium, 4 Log
        3 NoiseSet aside Log results and QoD (Quality of Detection) below 704 Log results; R17 (QoD [Quality of Detection] 30) to verify by hand
        4 VerifyRemove false positives with written reasonsR04 (Windows-only flaw on Linux) and R05 (backported fix)
        5 GroupOne remediation action per problem20 results become 16 actions
        6 PrioritizeScore = CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) + 3 (KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities]) + 1 (EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System] ≥ 0.10) + 2 (Internet) + criticality 1–3P1 ≥ 14 (7 days) · P2 ≥ 11 (30 days) · P3 ≥ 8 (90 days) · P4 (180 days)
        7 RecordWrite VS- rows with evidence for Lab 3scan_risk_factors.csv

(check on VirusTotal)

(check on VirusTotal)
